title: Between the Nodes
text:
About this book
This is a story, and it’s also the way you will learn the finite element method from AE 370. The story is fictional, but I hope you find truth behind the made up content, about human behavior and how it interacts with engineering.
You’ll read about one chapter before each class session. The mathematics lives inside the story: in the code the characters write, the plots they make, the emails they send, and the puzzles they can’t solve yet. Read it the way you would a mystery: notice what doesn’t add up, and keep going. Every number and every figure in the book is computed by real code, and the code is shown wherever a character looks at it.
The book builds on Lectures 16–17 (global spectral methods for BVPs). It doesn’t repeat them.

title: Between the Nodes
text:
Acknowledgments
To Tess, for loving stories with me, and for teaching me to understand what makes them worth telling.
This book was written with Claude, Anthropic’s AI model, as an extensively and iteratively used resource. The idea of teaching through a fictional story, its basic premise and key characters, the framing of the technical content, and the overall technical topic (the finite element method) were my choices, as were the Quarto book format and the flipped classroom in which students work through the course content in this narrative form. Over twenty-seven versions of back-and-forth, Claude was invaluable in fleshing out the characters; finalizing the narrative structure and its details; developing successively more detailed scene beats; drafting and refining prose; deciding the engineering setting and the boundary value problem around which the method is described; and proposing the numerical puzzles that give the story its whodunit elements.
— Andres Goza

title: 2:14 a.m.
text:
The ticket is eight days old. Add graded conductivity within a layer to the through-thickness solver. One sentence, from a manager who thinks of it as an afternoon’s work. Luis has spent several afternoons on it. Then the evenings. Well, not on the ticket itself. On something that could plausibly pass for work on the ticket, and that will give them, once it works, what the ticket should have asked for in the first place. It’s almost done. Well, almost almost. Now it is 1:40 in the morning and he has not added graded conductivity to anything.
He’s testing. That’s the defensible word for it. Before you change a code, you find out exactly what it does. He opens the reference case for the program’s new tile stack in his notebook: Kestrel, stack B. Ceramic tile on the hot side, structure on the cold side, and between them a bondline of adhesive 0.4 millimeters thick, thinner than anything the old stack designs used, because on a hypersonic airframe every gram is somebody’s argument.


from falkenrath import mara, ADHESIVE_LIMIT
from falkenrath import KESTREL_B as stack

T, log = mara.certify(stack)   # the certification workflow
peak = T.at(stack.adhesive_hot_face)
print(stack.name, "  polynomial degree:", T.degree)
print(f"peak adhesive T: {peak:.1f} K",
      f" (limit {ADHESIVE_LIMIT:.0f} K)")

Kestrel, stack B (thin bondline)   polynomial degree: 32
peak adhesive T: 417.5 K  (limit 440 K)



417.5 kelvin at the glue’s hot face, 23 under the adhesive’s limit. It’s the same number Mara’s code gave when this case went through certification. Good. The code does what it did yesterday.
He plots it anyway. He always plots it. A number is a summary, and a summary is somebody else deciding what you don’t need to see.


x = np.linspace(0, stack.thickness, 3000)
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3))
a1.plot(x, T.temperature(x))
a1.set(xlabel="depth (mm)", ylabel="T (K)")
a2.plot(x, T.flux(x))
a2.set(xlabel="depth (mm)", ylabel="heat flux")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The temperature is boring the way a temperature profile should be: hot at the surface, curving down through the tile, flattening out in the structure. The flux is not boring. Heat soaks into the tile near the surface and keeps flowing inward, so the flux should only grow with depth, a smooth ramp that levels off. Mara’s code draws the ramp, mostly. At each interface it misbehaves: it jumps, overshoots, and rings.
He knows this. Everyone who has opened Mara’s user notes knows this. Flux output near material interfaces is unreliable and should not be used. It does not affect the computed temperatures. A smooth polynomial asked to turn a sharp corner makes a mess of the corner. It’s one of the oldest artifacts there is.
His hand is already starting the next cell when he stops. The wiggles are kind of interesting. How far apart are they? And how does that spacing compare with the glue between the tile and the structure?
He zooms in on the bondline instead, and marks where the layers are.


x = np.linspace(20, 30, 3000)        # zoom on the bondline
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 3))
a1.plot(x, T.temperature(x))
a1.set(xlabel="depth (mm)", ylabel="T (K)")
a2.plot(x, T.flux(x))
a2.set(xlabel="depth (mm)", ylabel="heat flux")
for a in (a1, a2):
    layer_lines(a, stack.interfaces, shade=stack.adhesive)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()









The grey sliver is the glue.
The adhesive is a poor conductor, worse than the tile and far worse than the structure. Whatever heat comes out of the tile has to get through that sliver, and to push the same heat through a bad conductor you need a steep temperature drop across it. There should be a cliff in the temperature curve at the sliver.
The curve doesn’t even notice the sliver. It sails across as if the glue weren’t there. And the flux inside the sliver, the heat Mara’s code says is crossing the glue, is a fraction of what goes in on one side and comes out the other. Heat doesn’t disappear inside glue.
He sits back.
Mara’s code builds its answer out of a single polynomial that spans the whole stack, smooth everywhere, and a polynomial can only bend so sharply. At polynomial degree 32, the tightest turn it can make is a couple of millimeters wide; that’s what the ringing is, the polynomial overshooting a corner it can’t make. The glue is 0.4 millimeters. So the code isn’t approximating the glue badly. It can’t put a bend that narrow anywhere, so it has no way to put one where the glue is. As far as the polynomial is concerned, there is no glue.
It can’t see the glue.
No, that can’t be right. Mara’s code has been certified on these stacks. Its temperature at the glue converges; the check says so. Luis opens a new cell and runs a sweep in polynomial degree himself.


degrees = [16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128, 192, 256, 384, 512]
face = stack.adhesive_hot_face
sweep = [mara.solve(stack, degree=n).at(face)
         for n in degrees]
for n, Tn in zip(degrees, sweep):
    print(f"polynomial degree {n:4d}   {Tn:7.1f} K")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.semilogx(degrees, sweep, "o-")
ax.axhline(ADHESIVE_LIMIT, ls="--", c="gray")
ax.set(xlabel="polynomial degree",
       ylabel="adhesive hot face (K)")
plt.show()

polynomial degree   16     420.0 K
polynomial degree   24     418.0 K
polynomial degree   32     417.5 K
polynomial degree   48     417.3 K
polynomial degree   64     417.8 K
polynomial degree   96     419.7 K
polynomial degree  128     422.6 K
polynomial degree  192     430.1 K
polynomial degree  256     436.8 K
polynomial degree  384     440.9 K
polynomial degree  512     441.5 K










From polynomial degree 24 all the way to 96, the temperature at the glue barely moves: 417 to 420 kelvin. Flat, flat, flat. Then, past a hundred, it lifts off and climbs. By polynomial degree 384 it’s through the dashed line, the adhesive’s limit. By 512 it’s 24 kelvin above the certified number, and it still hasn’t stopped climbing.
The code isn’t converging toward the certified answer. Luis doesn’t notice that he’s breathing faster, or that his heart is pounding harder in his chest. What is happening?
He has to think for a second. What does the convergence check actually do? It’s the obvious one; anyone would think to use it. Start at polynomial degree 32, double it, compare the temperatures. If the two agree to within a kelvin, the answer has stopped moving, and you’re converged. If not, double again.
His hands moving faster on the keyboard, he pulls up the certification log for this case.



CERTIFICATION LOG  thermal / Kestrel stack B
  convergence check: double the polynomial degree until the
  temperature at the adhesive hot face changes by < 1.00 K
    degree  32 ->  64: 417.46 -> 417.78 K, change 0.32 K: PASS
  accepted polynomial degree 32



Polynomial degree 32 to 64: a third of a kelvin. Passed on the first step. And the sweep shows why. Mara’s code thinks it’s converged at polynomial degree 32, because doubling to 64 barely changes the temperature. But the two runs only agree because both are blind to the glue. Raise the polynomial degree until the glue comes into view, and the temperature lifts off and climbs toward something higher, over the adhesive’s limit.
He reads the log twice. Two runs, a factor of two apart in polynomial degree, agreeing to a third of a kelvin, and both of them at least twenty kelvin low; the sweep hasn’t finished telling him how much more.
He’s on his feet before he decides to stand. He catches himself pacing, and notices for the first time that his fingers are tingling. Mara’s code is certifying the new thin stacks, and it’s wrong.
He sits back down faster than he means to and opens the other window on his monitor, where the eight days have actually gone. He calls it Tent, after the shape of the functions it’s built from. Nobody else calls it anything; nobody else knows it exists. He built it because it’s the obvious way to handle the thin stacks. No reason to add a feature to a code that needs replacing. Build Tent first, then add graded conductivity to that.
But he hadn’t known that Mara’s code was flat-out wrong on the thin stacks. The whole time he’s been building Tent, he’s been able to hear the thermal analysts already: a grumpy, narrow-minded this isn’t the graded conductivity we asked for. He’s been gearing up for the battle he’d have to win before they’d let him help them.
He learned from the mesh-generator debacle that improvements come with battles. The old one fell apart at corners. Wherever a tile’s edge met the gap filler and the bondline, it threw out slivers, elements so thin and skewed that the solver either choked on them or quietly returned garbage, and the analysts spent days hand-fixing the corners on every new tile layout. It also took forty minutes to mesh a single panel. Luis rewrote the corner handling over a weekend: elements graded smoothly into every corner, and every element’s shape checked before it went out the door. No more slivers, no more hand-fixing, and a panel meshed in under two minutes.
He had walked in that Monday bright-eyed, so excited. He was sure they’d stop whispering, just loud enough for him to hear, about him fixing things that weren’t broken. He’d be part of the team, like everyone else. A part of the team they needed. Maybe even liked. Or if they didn’t like him, they’d at least start liking his code.
Instead he got a whiny rebellion. Little babies who couldn’t appreciate a better interface to go with the better algorithm. Instead of a thank-you, he spent hours of his workdays writing reports: every way the old mesher failed, every way the new one didn’t, and how much faster it was. And because he was right, and because it made their work better, and because Brandon made them, the analysts adopted the mesher. But the cost of helping them was clear too. The whispered complaints were now said out loud. Confident statements about his attitude, his inability to respect the team, passed around the office as if they were facts as hard as the better code he’d given them. He still doesn’t understand why he has to fight for every improvement.
Now, with Mara’s code doing what it does on these new stacks, he won’t need the battle. He won’t need to upset everyone to give them better code. They’ll finally just see it, say thank you, and ask for help getting onto Tent. Honestly, he doesn’t even need the thank-you. Just the basic respect that lets him contribute when he finds something he can improve.
He’s not naive, of course. He has to be careful. He remembers what Brandon told him after the mesher: the trouble with getting buy-in was that they didn’t understand why the old one was broken, or why his was better. Help them see it, and they’ll come around. So he’ll do it carefully, clearly. He’ll show them how Mara’s code breaks, and how Tent doesn’t.
Instead of one smooth polynomial across the whole stack, Tent cuts the stack into pieces, elements, with a node at every place the material changes, and builds the answer out of straight lines that each live on only one or two pieces. If the glue is 0.4 millimeters thick, it gets an element 0.4 millimeters wide. There is nothing for it not to see.
He runs Tent on stack B, the thin one, with the coarsest mesh that makes any sense: one element per layer. Three elements, four nodes. He derived the exact solution for this stack last week (a layered slab with exponential heating integrates cleanly, if tediously), and he checks Tent against it.


from falkenrath import tent, exact

Tt = tent.solve(stack, per_layer=1)
Te = exact(stack)
for x, Tx in zip(Tt.nodes, Tt.nodal):
    err = abs(Tx - Te.at(x))
    print(f"node {x:5.1f} mm   Tent {Tx:8.3f} K"
          f"   error {err:.1e} K")

x = np.linspace(0, stack.thickness, 1000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
ax.plot(x, Te.temperature(x), label="exact")
ax.plot(Tt.nodes, Tt.nodal, "o-",
        label="Tent, 1 element/layer")
ax.set(xlabel="depth (mm)", ylabel="T (K)")
ax.legend()
plt.show()

node   0.0 mm   Tent 1100.000 K   error 0.0e+00 K
node  24.0 mm   Tent  446.472 K   error 0.0e+00 K
node  24.4 mm   Tent  402.879 K   error 0.0e+00 K
node  40.0 mm   Tent  300.000 K   error 0.0e+00 K










Zero error at the glue’s hot face. At every face. Not small: zero, to the last digit double precision can hold. Three straight segments laid across a curve that is plainly not straight, and every node sitting dead on it. At the glue’s hot face, Tent says what Mara’s code, in the polynomial-degree sweep, was so incompetently crawling toward: 446 kelvin.
The number Mara’s code certified for this case is 29 kelvin low. The real temperature, which Tent gets exactly even at this comically coarse resolution, is over the limit. Four nodes got it right.
He’d seen the exactness before, on the thick legacy stacks and the textbook test cases he’d used to build Tent in the first place. Every node, dead on, every time. He’d expected the thin stack to be the hard test, the one that finally broke it. It didn’t break. Luis grins wide.
Luis opens his work email and starts a new message to the team. As he writes, his breathing slows, and for the first time tonight his heart stops pounding. There’s no arguing with this. It’s the fix the analysts needed and didn’t even know they needed. He knows it won’t happen overnight. But this is the first step toward his new era at Falkenrath-Voss.

title: Mara’s code
text:
The workbench had arrived on a Tuesday, in a box the size of a canoe, and Joyce had spent Wednesday assembling it with the confidence of a woman who knew what to do with a good set of instructions.
That was either why she had been a good engineer or why she hadn’t been a great one. Somewhere around the third Allen key she had decided not to settle which.
The bench stood where Sam’s bed used to be. The rest of the room was still mostly Sam: a corkboard of concert wristbands, a shelf of paperbacks with cracked spines, a box marked SAM — KEEP?? in Sam’s own handwriting, the question marks underlined, as if past Sam had foreseen exactly this morning and wanted no part of it. The plan was simple. Clear the room. Set up the bench. Build the guitar. Joyce had written the plan on an index card and put the card in a plastic sleeve, which was not the same as laminating it, she’d told Brandon. Brandon had laughed at her anyway, in the way only he could, which left her feeling appreciated rather than made fun of.
The guitar was in the corner, in a long, flat box labelled DREADNOUGHT KIT — SPRUCE / MAHOGANY — ADVANCED. She had chosen Advanced over Intermediate on the grounds that she had run a numerics group for twenty-two years and could surely manage some glue. The box was still sealed. That was correct. You don’t open the kit until the bench is ready, and the bench isn’t ready until the room is clear, and the room isn’t clear until someone decides about SAM — KEEP??
Her phone buzzed on the windowsill. Sam. She smiled at it, and thought, I’ll call back when I’ve finished this box, which she felt was a perfectly reasonable thing to think. She turned the phone face down, gently, the way you’d put down something you meant to come back to.
The doorbell rang at ten.
“You look retired,” Brandon said.
“I’m building a guitar.”
“Can you play?”
“That’s phase two.” She stepped back to let him in. “Come see my bench. It’s my opus. Forty years in numerics, and I’m only now realizing I was wasted there. I’m built for hands-on work.”
He chuckled in a way that made Joyce think he didn’t believe her. But he still admired the bench, which was kind of him, and the guitar kit, which was kinder. Then he stood in the doorway of the room with his hands in his jacket pockets, the way he used to stand in the doorway of her office when he had bad news and wanted credit for delivering it in person.
“It’s about Mara’s code,” he said.
Joyce took a second with that.
Mara had written that solver in her second year at Falkenrath, in a single spring, and it had outlived three programs, two reorganizations, and Mara’s own time at the company by a decade. Mara had been the best engineer Joyce ever worked with, and the one Joyce had lost. Not with a door slammed, but with a slow, polite drift that ended in a resignation letter and a card that said thank you for everything and meant it, which had somehow been worse.
Joyce kept a private list of the people she’d been lucky enough to watch get good. No: she was owning her accomplishments now. The people who had gotten really, gosh-darn good, and wouldn’t have without her. She felt a smile in her chest when she let herself admit the list was long. The other list, the ones she had tried and failed to help become great, was short. But it was the one she remembered best. That was just the arithmetic of a career, and she had mostly made her peace with it.
“Is it broken?” she said.
“That’s the question.” Brandon sat on the edge of the bench, which held him, as she had known it would. “You’ve heard about Kestrel.”
“Only that it exists, and that it’s been eating the budget since before I left.”
“It’s eating everyone’s budget. Reusable hypersonic vehicles. Not one flight and into the ocean: the same airframe, flying again and again, which means the heat shield has to come home in one piece every time and fly again.” He held up his hands a few inches apart. Joyce couldn’t tell whether he was showing her some feature of the heat shield or the margin for error. “Same idea as always: ceramic tile on the outside, bonded to the structure underneath. But every gram you carry on every flight is a gram you can’t spend on fuel or payload, so they’ve been shaving the thickness of every layer in the stack. Including the adhesive.” He stopped to blow out a breath, as if he’d been holding it too long. She had missed this about him. It was what made him a good boss: he could see how the whole picture had to come together for the next engineering marvel. More than see it; he couldn’t contain his excitement about it, and it was contagious. “On the new Kestrel stacks it’s under half a millimeter.”
She raised an eyebrow. “That’s thin. The old ones were…”
“Almost ten times that, in case you’ve forgotten since becoming a rock-star guitarist.” He seemed to realize he’d cut her off, and smiled an apology.
She didn’t mind. This was how the back-and-forth worked with them, and she liked it. “And I assume the adhesive still has to stay under its temperature limit, on the side against the hot tile.”
He nodded. “That’s the number the heat-shield design team builds its margins on. Peak adhesive temperature, straight from Mara’s code.” He rubbed his eyes. “Last week one of my people emailed the entire numerics list at two in the morning. The subject line was ‘Mara’s code can’t see the glue.’”
Joyce gave a warm half snort. “It’s punchy, that’s for sure.”
Brandon pointed a finger at her. “It’s terrible. Half the list thought it was spam. The other half wrote back to ask what glue.”
Joyce felt as if they were kids again, brother and sister, and he was mad because she’d laughed at him when their mom made him do an extra round of dishes. Not mad, really. It was a game they played. She would poke him in just the right places, and he enjoyed it so much he had to put on a persona, Mad Brandon, to react to her jabs. It was a strange way to show someone you liked talking to them. Stranger, maybe, that Joyce saw exactly what he was doing, liked it, and wanted to provoke it.
She let herself admit that she missed this. The fun problems, and the deeply flawed people who worked on them. It was the human side that had always pulled at her most. Any of these problems was solvable. Put the right person in the room (heck, the right LLM) and the answer falls out. But you don’t get any person in the room; you get the team you’ve got. And the most amazing part was that what stood between a team and the answer was almost never whether they were technically able. It was something someone had said to someone else three weeks ago, or baggage from a past marriage, or something they weren’t even aware of. Getting them to see it, and then move past it: that was the secret.
Brandon was watching her, waiting to see whether she’d take the bait. Maybe he had missed this too. He probably didn’t have many people who could both listen to him and prod him when he needed it. Or either one, really. He was plenty likeable, but likeable came with being the boss, and most people probably didn’t see how he hid behind the energy and the likeability. Coming up at the same time, with her a few years ahead, had helped Joyce see it. She had always been the older sister. When he was younger his enthusiasm had been rawer. He’d always had a knack for unsticking a stalled project by getting the right people talking to each other, or for getting one green-lit by upper management with an elevator pitch and a few beers at Lucky’s. But he’d also wanted to go all in on half-baked ideas that were exciting and had nothing underneath them yet. And sometimes his energy came out as a knee-jerk reply to a colleague, one better left until the next day. It had been one of the loveliest parts of Joyce’s career, watching him shave off the unhelpful parts and hone in on what made him who he was. She had never told him that. Maybe someday she would.
“Who’s the engineer?”
“Luis Arroyo. Two years in. You’d like him.” Brandon rocked on his heels. “He fixed an emissivity table we’d been using on every program for six years. It came from a supplier, for the tile coating, and he noticed the curve bent the wrong way at high temperature. Units error, right in the supplier’s spreadsheet. It saved a test article. Then he rewrote our mesh generator over a weekend because the old one annoyed him, and the new one’s better, and he didn’t tell anyone until it was done.” He paused. “Best numerical instincts I’ve seen since Mara.”
Brandon had never been subtle. Joyce watched a cheeky smile spread across his face. Sure, she was a little annoyed that he thought he was pulling her into some scheme he’d concocted. It was more annoying that it was working. But mostly it was fun.
“And the analysts?”
“Furious. Mara’s code has twenty years of successful flights behind it, and it passed its convergence check on the thin stack, and some kid with no manners says it’s wrong and his own code is exact, at two in the morning, to forty people.” Brandon spread his hands. “He’s not wrong often. But when he’s right, he’s right at people. Management’s started asking whether he’s a fit.”
“So you want me to tell you who’s right.”
“I want you to come in for a few weeks. Consult. Look at what he’s done, look at the code, talk to him.” He nodded at the room. “You’d have afternoons free for the guitar.”
Joyce looked at the sealed box. “If he’s as good as you say,” she said, “he’ll work it out.”
“He has worked it out. Maybe.” Brandon took a breath, and when he went on his voice had lost some of its lightness. “Nobody here can tell. And he’s going to get himself fired before anyone finds out.”
Brandon, she noticed, had saved that part for last. He’d known her for thirty years. He’d known the code wouldn’t be enough to get her into a car, and he’d known what would, and he’d put it at the end, where it would still be in the room after he left.
She could see the shape of the thing: somebody very good, on the way to making sure nobody ever found out how good. She had seen that shape many times, and she had been good at changing its ending. But she had also retired, partly, because she was tired of the times she hadn’t been. What if Luis became another name on the wrong list? Capable, probably smarter than she was, and red flags all over.
“I don’t know the details,” Brandon said, already moving toward the door. “I’ll forward you the email. You’ll be able to make better sense of it than anything I can tell you.”
“I haven’t said yes.”
Brandon paused and turned back to her.
“Read the email. Then you can tell me no.” He turned around again, walked out the door, and left.

The schedule on the refrigerator said 6:00 coffee. 6:15–8:00 bench. At 6:15 Joyce was at the bench, with her coffee, and with her laptop, which the schedule did not mention.
She had read the email once last night, the way she read anything after nine: to decide whether it was a morning problem. It was. She read it again now with her glasses on.
The subject line was terrible. It made her like Luis more. It was either written by someone completely certain or someone pretending to be. Either way, she was interested, the way some people find fireworks interesting: from a respectful distance, and with an eye on where the sparks were directed.
She skipped the attached flux plot. She knew what flux plots from that code looked like near an interface. She opened the second attachment, the sweep in polynomial degree, and looked at it for a long time.
The convergence check had passed. She knew the check; her group had written it. Start at polynomial degree 32, double it, compare the temperature at the glue; if the two answers agree to within a kelvin, the answer has stopped moving, so stop. If not, double again. In forty years, agreement had meant exactly one thing: you’re done, because the answer has arrived. And here was the same code agreeing with itself to a third of a kelvin at polynomial degrees 32 and 64, and going on agreeing with itself at much higher polynomial degree, until it shot off: 24 kelvin higher by polynomial degree 512, over the adhesive’s limit and still climbing.
She did one thing Luis hadn’t put in the email. She pulled the certification log for the stack A reference case, the old four-millimeter bondline every program before Kestrel had used. The same check, the same code, the same tolerance:



CERTIFICATION LOG  thermal / legacy stack A
    degree   32 ->   64   change in T  16.26 K   refine
    degree   64 ->  128   change in T   8.67 K   refine
    degree  128 ->  256   change in T   4.34 K   refine
    degree  256 ->  512   change in T   2.32 K   refine
    degree  512 -> 1024   change in T   1.13 K   refine
    degree 1024 -> 2048   change in T   0.56 K   PASS
  accepted polynomial degree 1024



On the thick stack, the check had refused to stop. It doubled its way up to polynomial degree 1024, the change in temperature halving each time, the way a converging answer should. On the thin stack it stopped at the first step.
How do two answers agree with each other and both be wrong?
She held the question for a while, because it deserved holding.
She closed her eyes and remembered Mara’s code. She saw Mara at a whiteboard in 2006, in a cardigan with chalk dust on one sleeve, explaining why she’d chosen integrated Legendre polynomials. Because then the slopes are orthogonal, Mara had said, and drawn the matrix for a single wall, nothing but a diagonal, and looked at Joyce as if this were the most obvious and most delightful thing in the world. Layers had cost the diagonal, conductivity inside the integral, every entry filled in, but a dense solve at degree 32 is nothing, and Mara had shrugged that off too.
So what had gone wrong now? It can’t see the glue. Joyce couldn’t tell whether Luis’s brashness amused or annoyed her. No, that wasn’t helpful. Understanding him was the important thing. Was he trying to piss people off? To impress them? To stun them into not arguing?
Impossible to say yet. Not enough information. Joyce pulled the notepad toward her. Mara’s functions were smooth, and every one of them spanned the whole stack.
How narrow a feature can a polynomial of degree 32 draw? Not narrower than the spacing of its own wiggles, which in the middle of the stack is about π/2n of the thickness (a polynomial’s zeros crowd toward the ends and spread out to about that spacing in the middle). She worked it out: 2.0 millimeters. The bondline was 0.4.
So the basis wasn’t approximating the bondline badly. It couldn’t represent anything that thin at all. The check compared the code with itself at two resolutions, and both were too coarse to see the glue. A paint roller and a slightly smaller paint roller will agree perfectly about a hairline: there isn’t one. Doubling the polynomial degree only tells you the answer has stopped changing. It can’t tell you whether it stopped because it arrived, or because it hasn’t started yet.
When should it start? When the wiggles got narrower than the glue: polynomial degree 157 or so, by her estimate. She checked it against Luis’s sweep. The temperature lifted off at around polynomial degree one hundred. And on the thick stack the glue had been wide enough to see from the very first step, so there the check had been honest all along.
Luis was right.
Joyce put the pen down and found that she was making a list, which she did when something impressed her and she didn’t yet know what to do about it. To see this, he’d had to plot a quantity nobody plots. Then sense that a problem everyone already knew about was hiding a worse one. Then connect it to the physical features of the new stacks. Then, hardest of all, distrust a check that had passed.
If someone had handed her this question (why does the check stop early on the thin stack?) she’d have had an answer by lunch. She was sure of that the way she was sure of very few things. Hand her a question and she would take it apart, every piece, and know where each one went.
But nobody had handed Luis a question. He had been asked to add a feature. He’d looked at a plot everyone had been told to ignore, and seen that it was a question, and that the question was the most important one in the building. That was the part she couldn’t do, or had never once done. Maybe those were the same thing. Forty years of answering questions beautifully. She couldn’t think of one she’d been the first to ask.
Then the last line of the email, alone in its paragraph like a man standing on a chair: Tent is exact at every interface.
Well, no. Nothing was exact. In forty years Joyce had met exactly one exact thing in numerical analysis, a boundary condition, and a fair amount of the time somebody had implemented it wrong. She underlined exact on the notepad, twice, and wrote ? next to it, and then, after a moment, how would that even work, and then she sat looking at that for longer than she meant to.
The clock on the laptop said 8:10. The bench hour was gone. The kit was still sealed.
She turned to a clean page and wrote Luis — at the top, and under it, the first of her questions.

Falkenrath-Voss had moved the numerics group up to the fourth floor since she’d left, which Joyce had decided not to take personally. Conference room 4C had a whiteboard someone had cleaned with real conviction and a window onto the parking structure. Luis Arroyo was already there.
He was younger than she’d pictured, and neater: pressed shirt, laptop open, and squared on the table in front of him, a printout of his own email. Below the email, in pencil, small and even, ran a column of notes. She couldn’t read them upside down, but she recognized the format. Responses to different lines of attack, prepared and ready to deploy.
He stood, shook her hand, sat. “If this is about the subject line,” he said, “I stand by it.”
His words came out short and hard. It wasn’t impolite, exactly, but he was ready for a fight. Interesting. Did he want that outcome, or was he worried she was going to start one? “Mr. Arroyo, I think everyone in this building knows you stand by that subject line.” She said it warmly, and smiled as she sat down across from him.
She turned her notepad around to face him, so he could see the page she’d filled at six that morning. “I read it. You’re right about the glue. The check never got out of the pre-asymptotic regime: thirty-two and sixty-four are both too coarse to see a layer that thin, so they agree with each other about the wrong answer.”
“Okay,” Luis said.
His eyes went to the printout and down the pencil column, item by item, the way you’d look through a toolbox for the right size wrench. There wasn’t one. He’d prepared for every objection but agreement. So he was better at being argued with than agreed with. Or more used to it? Either way, she didn’t know yet whether that was something to worry about or something to use. Probably both. Most things were.
“But Mara’s code isn’t wrong,” she said. “It’s blind at this degree. Raise the polynomial degree and it sees.”
“Raise it to what?” That came fast; that one was on the list. “The check can’t tell you. You’d need hundreds, and it’s a dense solve every time. And the flux never converges. Not at any degree.”
“I know about the flux.”
“Then you know the code can’t get the physics right at an interface. Ever.”
Joyce started to say that nobody signed off on flux, and stopped, because that was what the analysts had told him, and it wasn’t an answer. It was a procedure.
She looked at his screen instead: the flux near the glue, jagged and overshooting, wrong in a way that a higher polynomial degree would narrow but never cure, and beside it the temperature, the number everyone signed off on, smooth and, given enough degree, converging. She had known both of those facts for twenty years. She had never once set them side by side.
The temperature is built from the slope. Integrate the slope and you have the temperature; that’s all a temperature profile is. So if the slopes never settle near the interfaces, if the code gets them wrong at every degree, forever, what exactly is the temperature converging to? And why should it converge at all? Build a wall out of bad bricks and it shouldn’t be able to stand upright.
“Then how,” she said slowly, “is the temperature converging?”
Neither of them answered. Luis had stopped looking at his printout. He pulled the laptop back toward himself, opened the flux plot, zoomed in on the glue, zoomed again, typed something, frowned at it. It was the absorbed, slightly impolite focus of someone who has briefly forgotten there’s anyone else in the room. Joyce knew that kind of attention. She’d spent a career trying to point it at the right problems.
For the first time since she’d walked in, they were looking at the same thing. She noted that, near the top of the page: whatever else he was, he couldn’t leave a good question alone. If there was a door, that was it.
Why did the temperature converge when the flux didn’t? It was the right question, but they weren’t going to solve it this morning. Move him to the next topic. Why was he so set on not fixing Mara’s code? Did he need to do things his own way? Did he want credit for building something new? Or did he really just think he’d found something better? “If raising the degree rescues the temperature,” she said, “why do we need Tent?”
He looked up. “Because you’d need hundreds of degrees and a dense matrix to see a layer you could just put a node on.” He was quicker now; that one was on the list too. “Tent puts a node at every interface. The resolution follows the stack, not the polynomial. The glue is one element, however thin it is. The matrix is tridiagonal. And the adhesive’s hot face is a node, so the number you sign off on is exact.”
All right. All defensible. But was that the motive? “So the resolution follows the geometry instead of the basis.”
“That’s what I said.”
It was, more or less. She’d restated it anyway, out of forty years’ habit, the way you might straighten a picture in someone else’s house. Mara used to hate that too. She let herself observe the thought come and go, then brought her attention back to Luis.
“Exact is a big word,” she said.
He turned the laptop around. One element per layer: three straight segments laid across the temperature profile, the true curve bowing above them through the tile. Below the plot, the errors at the four nodes. Zeros. Not small numbers. Zeros. This figure hadn’t been in the email. Had he had it the whole time? Why hadn’t he sent it? Was he afraid it would upset people? Did he want to upset them, by making the claim and holding back the proof? Or maybe he’d only made it this morning.
She had underlined exact twice that morning and written how would that even work. Now she looked at the zeros for a long moment and did the honest thing, which was to stop doubting them. The straight segments missed the curve everywhere except at the nodes, and at the nodes they missed it by nothing at all.
“I don’t know why that’s true,” she said.
That got a look, quick and surprised. Or was it anger? No, she didn’t think so. Did he just not expect anyone to care about the technical meat of his work?
“Why is it?”
“It fits slopes.” He shrugged. “It’s obvious if you draw it.” He didn’t draw it. He had gone back to his laptop, presumably to the question of why the temperature converged.
Obvious, Joyce thought, was either a step he’d skipped or a door he was keeping shut, and she didn’t know him well enough yet to tell which. It was the second time that morning he’d used a word to close a subject. She noted that too.
What she did know was how the next six months went if nothing changed. The analysts would keep answering his tone instead of his plots, and he would keep answering their tone instead of their questions, and one day somebody senior would decide the plots weren’t worth the tone.
She tried something. Not a lesson; she had never once seen a lesson land on anybody. Just a true sentence, set down where he could pick it up or leave it.
“Right now,” she said, “you’re the only person in this building who can check you. That’s a lonely place to be right.”
He didn’t answer. His face did nothing in particular. He might have heard it, or filed it under things retired managers say. She’d find out, or she wouldn’t, and either way it would tell her something.
“Send me everything you’ve run,” she said. “Notebooks, scratch work, dead ends. The messy ones too.”
“The messy ones aren’t—”
“Especially the messy ones.” She capped her pen. “I want to see how you got here, not just where you landed.”
That got the nearest thing to a smile she’d seen all morning.

After he’d gone, Joyce stayed in 4C with the parking structure and the clean whiteboard and took stock, the way she used to after a first meeting, back when first meetings were her job.
Column one, what he could do. The diagnosis, which she’d already been over at six a.m. Tent, the natural next move, made before anyone asked. Pictures, with real mathematics behind them. And at two in the morning he had written the most important email the thermal group had received in a decade, and made it almost impossible to read.
Column two, how he was making sure nobody noticed. Rebuttals in pencil. Answers to questions she hadn’t asked. Obvious, twice. Closing subjects with definitive words that explained nothing. More ready for an argument than for agreement.
Column three, which she always kept smaller than she wanted to: guesses. Under it she wrote More responsive to interest? That would hardly be surprising. Everyone wants people to care about what they have to say and what they’ve built. Still, it felt like the closest she had gotten to him, underneath the prickly exterior he used to keep people away. She drew an arrow from it and added Work dismissed because of tone? Neither explained how absorbed he’d gotten when she asked why the temperature converged. She moved her pen a few lines down and added one more: Genuine interest in the math.



what he can do
the diagnosis (right)
Tent, before anyone asked
pictures, real math behind them
the 2 a.m. email: most important in a decade


how he hides it
rebuttals in pencil
answers to questions I didn’t ask
obvious (×2)
closes subjects instead of explaining
ready for an argument, not agreement


guesses
More responsive to interest?
↳ Work dismissed because of tone?
 
Genuine interest in the math



She nodded at the list, then gave herself a quick shake of the head. Probably completely off base. She underlined guesses, faintly, and closed the notepad, as if someone might see them and be disappointed in how wrong she’d gotten him.
Mara would have liked him, she thought, and then, more carefully: Mara would have recognized him. The certainty was different. Mara’s had been quiet, something she hid behind; his was loud, something he swung. But Mara would have listened to what he had to say; that much was certain. Would she have understood his one-liners, the ones that walled him off? They were almost opposites there. Mara fell so deeply into an algorithm that her reports ran five times longer than they needed to, with more detail than anyone wanted, let alone asked for. That hadn’t worked either. No. Joyce didn’t want to think about that.
Joyce blinked a few times and felt the pressure of her fingertips against the pen. Index finger, thumb, middle finger. She noticed which part of each one pressed against it. Then she let her mind go where it had been trying to go for an hour: four dots, dead on a curve that wasn’t straight. It fits slopes. On a clean page she drew a curve, and a straight line underneath it, and sat turning the pen over in her fingers.

title: Better than good
text:
It’s 11:40 at night, and Luis has had Joyce’s email open since four.


From: Joyce Abernathy
To: Luis Arroyo
Subject: everything


Notebooks, scratch work, dead ends. The messy ones too. No rush, but I’m up early.
— J


No rush, but I’m up early. That’s a deadline. He knows a deadline when it’s being polite.
He opens a new notebook, names it for_joyce.ipynb, looks at the empty first cell, and doesn’t type anything. Instead he does the thing he’s been not doing for a week. He opens the thread.


From: Dennis Hale, Senior Thermal Analyst
To: thermal-numerics@falkenrath-voss.com
Subject: RE: Mara’s code can’t see the glue


This code has twenty years of successful flights behind it. A plot of an output we explicitly don’t use is not evidence. Please don’t send things like this to the full list.




From: Kurt Sorensen
To: thermal-numerics@falkenrath-voss.com
Subject: RE: Mara’s code can’t see the glue


The convergence check passed. That’s what it’s for.




From: Brandon Kowalczyk
To: Luis Arroyo
Subject: RE: Mara’s code can’t see the glue


Let’s talk before you send anything else to the list.


There are eleven more like the first two. None about the sweep.
He reads them in order, then out of order, as if they might read differently in another order.
None of them is about the plot. They’re about the time stamp. The list. The tone. The code’s age. Twenty years of successful flights. On thick bondlines, on stacks where the glue is four millimeters wide and a polynomial can see it. That’s the point. That was the whole point of the email. The convergence check passed. That’s what it’s for. Yes. And it passed because both of its runs were blind. That’s the other point. It was in the email too, in one sentence, with a plot attached.
He did exactly what Brandon told him to do after the mesher. He showed them. The sweep, the zoom, the reason in one paragraph. Nobody has to read a report to see a curve go through a dashed line.
And Brandon, to him alone: Let’s talk before you send anything else to the list. Luis knows what let’s talk means. Last time it meant three weeks of reports. It means somebody has already decided the problem is him.
He opens a reply and types: If anyone on this list can read a semilog plot, I’m happy to walk them through the part where the number goes over the limit. He reads it twice. It’s good. It’s exactly right, and it would get him fired by Friday. He deletes it one word at a time, so he can enjoy each word on its way out.
At two in the morning last week he’d thought the hard part was over. He’d thought that this time the evidence was so clear it would do the arguing for him. The first step toward a new era. He actually thought the words new era, in his own head. Luis closes his eyes, and a groan comes out of him before he can stop it.
Is it him? He’s been sure that everyone around him is literally stupid. Unable to read hard, objective facts put right in front of them. Either incompetent or deliberately blockheaded. The mesh generator all over again. And now Brandon’s email, just to him.
Brandon presumably isn’t sending one-off emails to the thermal analysts. Could this somehow be his fault? He really can’t see how. But he believes in data, and the data seems to point one way.
Well, not all the data. The meeting with Joyce in 4C comes back to him, and it doesn’t fit with any of this.
She agreed with him. First thing, before she’d even sat down properly: You’re right about the glue. He’d had a whole column of answers ready, and none of them were for that. Then she asked about the math. Not the tone, not the list: how it worked. She said I don’t know why that’s true out loud, in a conference room, like it cost her nothing. Nobody at Falkenrath-Voss has asked him how anything works. Not once, in two years.
And then: Right now, you’re the only person in this building who can check you. That’s a lonely place to be right.
His first reaction, in the room, was that it was a compliment. The only person who can check him. Wasn’t that the point? Only one person can be right in an argument. It’s lonely by design. His second reaction, on the drive home, was that she hadn’t said it like a compliment. She’d said it the way you’d point out a loose wire. He has turned it over every way since, and it won’t sit still.
What if there’s something he can’t see either?
He sniffs sharply, as if he could push the thought out through his nose. Then he does what he always does when he needs somewhere else to put his head. He works.
The notebook is for her. She’s the one reader who might judge it on what’s in it, which means it has to be undebatable. No gaps. No obvious. And it has to start where she starts, which is Mara’s code. Twenty years of running it. She doesn’t need Tent explained from scratch. She needs to know what’s different, and that turns out to be one thing.

1. What Tent is
Tent is Mara’s method with one change.
Same BVP: \(-(k\,u')' = f\) through the stack, with the hot-face and cold-face temperatures carried by a known function, the way Mara’s code carries them. Same three steps:

Choose a subspace \(\mathcal{V}\) and a basis for it.
Make the residual orthogonal to \(\mathcal{V}\): \(\;(f + (k\,u_a')',\, b_k) = 0\;\) for every basis function \(b_k\). Integrate by parts (the face terms drop out), and that’s \(\;\sum_j c_j\,a(b_j, b_k) = (f, b_k)\), with \(a(b_j, b_k) = \int k\,b_j'\,b_k'\,dx\).
Solve the linear system for the coefficients.

Mara chose \(\mathcal{V}\) = polynomials of degree \(n\) across the whole stack. Every one of her basis functions spans all 40 mm, smooth from the hot face to the cold one. Nothing in that subspace can bend inside 0.4 mm, so nothing in it can see the glue. Steps 2 and 3 were never the problem.
Tent changes step 1, and only step 1. Its subspace is built the finite element way, which makes Tent a finite element method.

He reads it back. Good. Under the notation, the recipe is short. Every equation is one test: take the residual, weigh it against one basis function, and require the result to be zero. One test per basis function, and one unknown coefficient per basis function, so the system always comes out square. That’s the whole method.
She knows steps 2 and 3 better than he does; her group ran them for twenty years. The only thing new to her is step 1, and step 1 is all about polynomials built locally, on a chopped-up version of the domain itself.
So step 1 doesn’t start with functions. It can’t. It starts with the stack. Mara’s subspace could be written down without knowing anything about the stack: polynomials of degree \(n\), done. Tent has to cut the stack into pieces first, elements, joined at nodes. In principle the nodes can go anywhere, as many as you like. But the obvious place for them is every place the material changes. That’s the one thing Mara’s code can’t do: her polynomials live on the whole stack at once, and can’t treat one stretch of it differently from another. So Tent puts its nodes at the material edges.


from falkenrath import tent, KESTREL_B as stack

nodes = tent.solve(stack, per_layer=1).nodes  # at interfaces
for e in range(len(nodes) - 1):
    a, b = nodes[e], nodes[e + 1]
    print(f"element {e+1}: {a:4.1f} -> {b:4.1f} mm,"
          f" width {b-a:4.1f} mm")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 1.4))
names = ["tile", "glue", "structure"]
for a, b, name in zip(nodes[:-1], nodes[1:], names):
    ax.axvspan(a, b, alpha=0.5 if name == "glue" else 0.15,
               color="gray")
    ax.text((a + b) / 2, 0.55, name, ha="center")
ax.plot(nodes, 0 * nodes, "ko")
ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1); ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("depth (mm)")
plt.show()

element 1:  0.0 -> 24.0 mm, width 24.0 mm
element 2: 24.0 -> 24.4 mm, width  0.4 mm
element 3: 24.4 -> 40.0 mm, width 15.6 mm










Three elements, four nodes. The tile is one element, 24 millimeters wide. The glue is one element too, 0.4 millimeters wide, 60 times narrower than the tile next to it: at this scale, two dots nearly on top of each other. Mara’s polynomial had to stretch across all of it. Here the glue gets an element of its own, and the element doesn’t care how thin it is.
He starts the next markdown cell.

2. The subspace
The solution lives in the space of

And stops.
The space of what? Continuous functions that are straight on every element. True. But it doesn’t say why. It’s the kind of sentence that comes back with and? written next to it. Why straight lines? Why not something even simpler? Why continuous? What does that buy you, and why should she believe it’s enough? To him the answers are obvious. What he doesn’t have is the sentence that makes the questions unnecessary.
He knows where he first heard it said that way, though. A room that smelled like whiteboard markers, junior year, and a man who never once let a sentence get away with being merely true.

Junior year
Room 112 of the Halston State engineering building had been renovated, according to a plaque by the door, in 1987. It felt older, despite the fresh floor wax. The seats in the third row leaned back a few degrees further than they were meant to. Luis sat there anyway. The third row was close enough to read Pruitt’s handwriting and far enough back that Pruitt had to look for you.
Dr. Pruitt never started with a review. Finally, someone who gave the students some credit. Every other professor spent minutes, literally minutes, at the start of every lecture reminding people what they’d just covered, how it fit into the bigger picture, what came next. Bro, we were there. Pruitt didn’t waste their time. He walked in, picked up a marker, and started.
“Last time,” he said, writing as he talked, “you solved a boundary value problem with polynomials defined on the whole domain. Each one was defined without reference to any particular place in it. Today we do it the other way around. We cut the domain first. Then we decide what a function is allowed to do on each piece.” Under the words he drew the domain, and then the cuts: a line, with dots where the pieces met.

mesh first, functions second









nodes \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_n\)  ·  elements \([x_{k-1}, x_k]\)

Luis knew that picture. It was the grid from finite differences, five weeks back: the same dots, the same spacing. He liked that more than he expected to. Something old, made to do something new.
“In a spectral method with global polynomials,” Pruitt went on, “you could write the subspace down before you knew anything about the domain. Polynomials of degree \(n\). Done.” He wrote it, and crossed it out. “Here, the subspace cannot even be stated until the mesh is. For the second-order boundary value problem we’ve been working on, for example, the most common choice is this,” and he leaned in to the board to write it.

\(\mathcal{V}_n = \{\, v \;:\; v\) continuous, linear on each element, \(v(a) = v(b) = 0 \,\}\)

“Is it a subspace? Three checks. You have three minutes.” Pruitt capped the marker and folded his arms with his back to the board, the way he did when he meant to wait the full three minutes even if everyone finished in one. It was the one concession he made. No reviews at the start of class, no hand-holding homework (his homework was properly hard). But he gave class time to working out the basics.
Around Luis, pencils. Two seats over, someone drew axes. Luis didn’t need to. He could see it was a subspace. He pictured two functions, each a string of straight segments pinned to zero at both ends, bending only at the dots. Add them. A segment plus a segment is a segment. The bends stay at the dots. Zero plus zero is zero.











Done. The zero function was obviously in. Scaling was the same picture, taller. He leaned back and looked at the clock: two minutes and forty seconds left.
Two minutes and forty seconds is a long time to spend on a line plus a line. He spent it the way he often did when he was bored in class, doing arithmetic he didn’t want to do. Tuition here, minus his scholarship. Tuition at the other school that had said yes, the one whose name people said a little slower, in hushed tones, like they were in church, minus the aid it had offered, which came nowhere close. Plus his mother’s catering van, which didn’t drive itself to weddings on Saturdays.
No. Luis blinked and stopped himself. Self-indulgent pity party. He looked back up at the board. Could he guess what Pruitt would write next?
It wasn’t only the mesh that was like finite differences. The functions were going to depend on the grid too. In finite differences, the little polynomials slid along with whichever point you were working at; these looked like they’d be pinned to points on the domain as well. But how? And how would that be any different from finite differences?
He checked the clock. One minute. Guessing Pruitt’s next move was a much better game.
He thought back. Finite differences made the differential equation hold at each grid point, with the derivatives swapped for differences. But this was coming out of the spectral methods, so it had to start from a weak form instead. He couldn’t see all the details yet, but it was a start. So then—
“Time,” Pruitt said. Oh, come on. He’d almost had it.
Pruitt went through the three checks in order, exactly as the notes had them. Luis watched him and thought, not for the first time, that Pruitt taught like a man who’d expected to be doing it somewhere else.
Then Pruitt turned to the room. “Now. Why lines?” On the mesh he drew a function that was flat on every element, a constant instead of a line, and jumped at every dot: a staircase. “These are even more local. One number per element. Easier to integrate. Why not these?” And through the staircase, two quick dashed strokes: an X.











The kind of silence where everyone finds something in their notebook that keeps their eyes off Pruitt’s.
“They jump,” Luis said. He hadn’t raised his hand. He had never spoken in this class before, or in any other at Halston. Luis found himself wondering why he’d answered now. Because, he decided, this was the first class that deserved it. The first one that trusted its students to think for themselves and do hard things.
Pruitt turned around. “And?”
“And the integral term needs a slope. A step doesn’t have one at the jump.”
A pause, long enough for Luis to replay the answer, check it for mistakes, and find none.
“Name.”
“Luis Arroyo.”
“Mr. Arroyo. I defined this subspace \(\mathcal{V}_n\) for the rod equation. What if we were instead dealing with a beam?”
Pruitt’s voice didn’t rise at the end, the way it would for a genuine question. It was a test. “The integral needs two derivatives now,” Luis said. “So the slope can’t jump either. Lines won’t do it.”
“Correct,” Pruitt said. “Both times.” He let that sit for exactly one second. “Now say the first one properly.”
Behind Luis, somebody gave a small cough. “I did.”
“You said it so that the people in this room understood it. Say it so that a referee can’t misunderstand it.”
Luis looked at the staircase on the board. He had said it. The jump, the slope, the integral: that was the whole thing. Pruitt didn’t want a better answer. He wanted the same answer in fancier words.
“The weak form for the rod equation,” Luis said slowly, “puts one derivative on each function. Piecewise constants don’t have a derivative at the nodes.”
“Better.” Pruitt wrote it on the board word for word and underlined weak form. “Say it that way the first time, Mr. Arroyo, and people will believe you the first time.” He capped the marker. “Next time: a basis.”
Class over. No fanfare. Pruitt set the marker in the tray, went to the desk, bent over it, and started writing on a sheet of paper.

7. Why the nodes are exact
Galerkin makes the residual orthogonal to every tent. In the weak form Tent actually solves, after integrating by parts, that says \[\int k\,(u - u_a)'\,b_k'\,dx = 0 \quad\text{for every } k.\] Now look at what’s in that integral. A tent’s slope is a constant on each of its two elements. So on each element, the integral is just a constant times the slope of the error, added up across the element, and adding up a slope across an element gives the rise across it. Orthogonality to a tent only ever sees how much the error rises across each element. It’s blind to what the error does in between.
Tent’s lines can’t follow the curve between the nodes, and they don’t have to. What a line can do is rise across its element by exactly what the true temperature rises there. Do that on every element, and the error rises by zero across each one, so every orthogonality condition holds. Galerkin has exactly one answer, so that’s the answer. Start at the hot face, where the temperature is fixed, and add up the rises: every node lands on the curve.

q = exact(thick).flux(x)
for deg in (64, 128, 256, 512):
    err = mara.solve(thick, degree=deg).flux(x) - q
    peak, l2 = abs(err).max(), trapezoid(err**2, x)
    print(f"degree {deg:3d}:  peak error {peak:.2f}"
          f"   integral of error^2 {l2:.3f}")

degree  64:  peak error 3.80   integral of error^2 1.855
degree 128:  peak error 3.68   integral of error^2 0.902
degree 256:  peak error 3.63   integral of error^2 0.454
degree 512:  peak error 3.67   integral of error^2 0.239



There it is. The peak barely moves: 3.8, 3.7, 3.6, 3.7. Double the polynomial degree as many times as you like and the spike at the interface stays just as tall. But it gets narrower, so the integral of its square halves every time the degree doubles. The error in the slope goes to zero on average, even though at the interface it never goes to zero at all.
So that’s what’s being forgiven: a spike that never shrinks, in a region that keeps getting thinner. And the temperature is the slope added up, so it inherits the small integral and not the tall spike.
It’s half an answer. He can see that it happens. He can’t see why the method is entitled to it: why a Galerkin solution would accept a permanent spike in exchange for a small integral, why that’s the trade it makes and not some other. He tries for an hour. He gets close enough to feel the shape of it, the way he felt the shape of the first row at the board, and no closer.
At 4:30 he reads the cell back as carefully as he can, as Joyce will read it. A question, a table, and a paragraph that stops in the middle of an idea. It isn’t perfect. But it’s more than he knew before. Surely it’s more than Joyce knew when she asked. It would give her something new to work from.
Is that enough? It’s so late it’s early now, and his mind drifts to a hotel ballroom, and to standing in front of an easel for hours.

Senior year, April
The undergraduate research symposium was in the ballroom of the Halston Marriott, on folding easels in rows, under chandeliers that had seen better weddings. Luis’s poster was mostly pictures. Vortex shedding behind a cylinder, in a water tunnel he’d built from a sixty-gallon fish tank and a pool pump, with food dye for the flow, his phone for a camera, and a script that tracked the vortices frame by frame. The vortices peeled off one side and then the other, in a street as regular as a heartbeat, and at the bottom of the poster sat a Strouhal number that matched the textbook.
It won.
He hadn’t let himself expect it, and then it happened, and for a while he didn’t know what to do with his hands. Professors he’d never had came by to shake one of them. The department chair said remarkable. Somebody took a photo.
And under all of it, a thing he’d never said to anyone: so I could have. The other school, the one that had said yes. He’d never known whether he’d have made it there, and there was no way to find out; you don’t get to run that experiment. He’d worked weekends in the van and nights on this, with a fish tank and a pool pump. This was as high as he could have gone with what he had. And it was the top. Maybe he’d belonged there after all. Maybe Halston had just been a detour the world made him take, and now it was over.
Pruitt came last. He stood at the poster longer than anyone had, reading all of it, the way he read a board. Luis waited.
Pruitt put one finger on the bottom corner. “Your Strouhal number has three significant figures and no error bar.”
Then, quietly, so that only Luis heard it: “They’ll see where you’re from and assume you’re not good enough. So be better than good.”
And he walked away, toward the coffee.
Luis stood next to his poster with the ribbon still on it. The pictures were the same pictures. The number at the bottom had three significant figures and no error bar, and now it was the only thing on the poster he could see. Where you’re from. He’d been from somewhere else for about ten minutes. Now he was from Halston again, and Pruitt had just told him he always would be.

He didn’t hear it as kindness then. It took the poster away from him.
At his kitchen table, he half-hears it as kindness now. That’s worse.
Better than good. No holes. He looks back at the last cell. The non-answer about why Mara’s code converges in temperature but never in flux. He still doesn’t know which reader Joyce is. If she’s the kind one, the half-answer costs him nothing. If she isn’t, it costs him the one person in the building who asked how anything works.
He selects the cell, the question and the table and the paragraph that stops, and deletes it.
At 5:04 he attaches the notebook to an email with no message in it and sends it to Joyce. Everything he’s run. Everything except the one messy thing he still can’t tidy up. Nobody asks for the messy stuff and means it.

title: The messy ones
text:
The notebook arrived at 5:04 in the morning, and Joyce, who was up at 5:30 regardless, found it waiting for her like a cat at the door.
By 6:40 she had read it twice: once fast, the way you read anything the first time, to find out what kind of thing it is; and once slowly, on paper, at the bench, with the notepad and a pencil. She had printed all fourteen pages for the second read; she liked paper. The bench had not been used for its intended purpose in nine days. The guitar building kit sat in its corner, still sealed, being patient in a way she found faintly accusatory.
She went through the notebook again in her head, the way she used to walk a design review: not what each part said, but what each part was for. The method, set up as a single change to Mara’s, so that it met Joyce exactly where she was coming from. The mesh, with a node at every material edge and the glue as an element of its own. The subspace, and why it had to be built from pieces of straight lines for this problem. The tents, formulas first and then the picture. Their role as a basis, proved. The matrix entries, worked out one element at a time. The assembly, adding up every element’s contribution. The solve, coded clearly and shown to match the exact answer at every node, as he’d already shown her in room 4C. And a lovely visual explanation, backed by written reasoning, for why the answer is exact at the nodes.
Clean, complete, in the right order. She’d had senior engineers who couldn’t do that with a month and a template. She admired it, and found, a little to her surprise, that the admiration didn’t sting. She loved having a question answered clearly, completely, understandably. And this time, she was the one who had asked the question. Come to think of it, she had done that a great deal over the years: asked the question that got someone to the right answer. She let herself enjoy that for a moment.
Then she moved her attention past the mathematics.
She had three pieces of evidence on Luis Arroyo now, and they didn’t agree. The email: either built to inflame or a very poor attempt at being understood, and nearly impossible to read either way. The meeting in room 4C: obviously competent, and dismissive, and incomplete; obvious, twice, where an explanation should have been. And now this: twenty-odd cells, an authoritative and complete treatment of the subject. Could the same person have written that subject line and this? Well, yes; one person had. Which meant the email hadn’t been incapacity. Then what was it?
And the timestamp. She had asked for what he had, and she had meant it. Nobody had asked him to do this overnight. He had done it overnight anyway, and done it like this.
She wrote 5:04 on the notepad and drew a box around it, which was what she did with numbers she didn’t know what to do with.
Then she went through it the slow way, cell by cell, and the first thing that snagged was cell 5.
The basis proof. Correct, complete, and written out in symbols, a little stiffly, like something translated from another language. Everywhere else in the notebook, pictures did the arguing: the mesh drawn to scale, the lopsided tents on the real stack, the slopes laid over each other. He thought in pictures; she’d watched him do it in 4C, reaching for the laptop instead of a sentence. And here, at the one place in the notebook where something had to be proved, there was no picture at all. A picture would have been a proof here, and the best kind. She knew exactly what he would have drawn. Why hadn’t he drawn it?
She didn’t guess. Not yet. She wrote cell 5: no picture? and went on.
Cell 7 she read three times. Why the nodes are exact. It was good. Orthogonality to a tent only sees how much the error rises across each element, because a tent’s slope is a constant there; a straight line can match a rise exactly; so every node lands. She felt the click of it. And under the click, something small that didn’t quite sit right. On each element, the integral is just a constant times the slope of the error. In the margin of the printout she wrote a constant: which constants? and made herself leave it there. She had an open question of her own, older than this one, and it had seniority.
It was only when she reached the end that she noticed what wasn’t there.
Notebooks, scratch work, dead ends. The messy ones too. She had said it in 4C, and again in writing. There were no messy ones. No dead ends, no scratch, no cell that started an idea and gave up on it. Every cell was finished. Not just thorough, not just well explained: polished. And, now that she looked for it, limited to the things he could be certain of. That pulled at her as much as anything in the notebook itself.
She turned back in the notepad to the page from 4C.

The narrow column on the right was the one she wanted. She went down it the way she’d go down a test matrix, one row at a time, with a green pen this time, so that she could tell later what she’d thought then from what she thought now.
More responsive to interest? Twenty careful cells, for the one person who had asked him how it worked, asked and meant it. A few terse sentences in room 4C, for an audience he’d expected to be hostile. One inflammatory line, for forty people he’d already decided wouldn’t read it; or for forty people who really had decided not to, and had answered his email accordingly, which came to much the same thing. Probably yes. Not definitive, but worth a tick.
Work dismissed because of tone? Nothing in the notebook could test that. She left it alone.
Genuine interest in the math. Cell 7 answered that. You don’t find orthogonality only sees the rise by accident at three in the morning.
And then a new line, from cell 5, with nothing behind it but the shape of a missing picture: someone taught him a picture doesn’t count? She kept the question mark.
A list of guesses is only as good as the evidence you haven’t looked at yet. So she made herself look for what was missing.
Her question about Mara’s code. Why does the temperature converge when the flux never does? It wasn’t anywhere in the notebook. Not a cell, not a sentence.
She didn’t believe for a moment that he hadn’t worked on it. In 4C he had started on it before she’d finished asking. She had watched him pull the laptop back, zoom in on the flux at the glue, zoom again, type something, frown at it, and forget for a minute that she was in the room. Some people go that deep into a question in a meeting and then leave it alone for a whole night. Not the person who had written the notebook she’d just read twice. He had worked on it. And whatever he’d found, he hadn’t sent it.
So the absence was information. One more line in green, at the bottom of the column. Then she looked over the page as it stood now.
